newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-U.S. Iran/Libya bill comes under more fire.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-U.S. Iran/Libya bill comes under more fire.

text.p: Unliteral sanctions imposed by the United States on Iran and Libya were condemned on Tuesday by all sides, including a former senior White House official.

But an aide to Senator Alfonse D'Amato, who sponsored last year's U.S. sanctions bill against foreign companies investing in the two oil producing nations slammed European nations for not backing the measures.
"If our friends in Europe wish to deal with the devil then so be it. Europe can either be part of the problem or part of the solution," said Gregg Rickman, D'Amato's legislative director.
President Clinton earlier this year signed the Iran/Libya sanctions bill designed to punish foreign companies which invested in Iran and Libya, a so-called secondary boycott.
The U.S. has already imposed a comprehensive trade ban preventing American companies dealing with the two countries.
Speaking at the annual Oil and Money conference in London, Rickman singled out France for "over-eager trade" and Germany for letting Tehran off lightly with cheap loans.
"Europe would rather turn a blind eye than lose business opportunities," he said.
But a former aide to President Carter during the 1979 Iranian hostage crisis warned that the measures would do little to combat terrorism and threatened to backfire if oil supplies run short.
"There is no evidence whatsoever that the actions taken will remedy those problems," said Gary Sick, now a director at New York's Columbia University.

"The effect of imposing a ban on Iran has been to reduce spare (oil output) capacity in the world," he said. "I would argue that if we have another oil crisis people will discover these sanctions were counterproductive."
Sick said he supported Europe's "constructive dialogue" with states like Iran and Libya, which would prove more productive.

"There is a dialogue between Europe and Iran in which differences of opinion are discussed in very clear terms and we prefer that," said Guy Arlette, oil and gas director at the French industry ministry.
"These laws are not in accordance with international law. We are going to react - it is underway," he added.
The European Union is waiting to make its case against the U.S. on the sanctions at a World Trade Organisation (WTO) hearing.
A senior official of the National Iranian Oil Corp (NIOC) said Iran appeared guilty until proven innocent in U.S. eyes.
"Somehow the U.S. always tries to link terrorism with Iran," said Hamid Moussavi, NIOC's international affairs advisor.

Moussavi and others warned that less than 25 years after the first oil price shock the West was staring another in the face, this time of its own making and not because of Arab boycotts or revolutions.

With about 220 billion barrels of proven oil reserves, or 22 percent of the world's total, under some form of sanctions, supply may fail to keep pace with surging demand, said Issam Al-Chalabi, consultant and Iraqi oil minister at the time of the 1990 invastion of Kuwait.
"The impact might not be felt now, but certainly in later years and that will certainly cause considerable shortage, instability as well as sharp fluctuation in prices," he told the conference.
"Can the world oil industry afford such a margin by sanctioning such capabilities, and for how long and at what price?" said Chalabi, who heads an independent consultancy in Oman.
United Nations and U.S. sanctions against Iraq, Iran and Libya were sowing the seeds of future oil market instability by preventing the development of new production capacity, he said.
Iran's Moussavi told delegates by early in the next millenium further incremental oil supply will have to be provided from the Middle East and Central Asia.
"The world can not afford the luxury of embargoing millions of barrels of oil production in the very near future," he said.
Moussavi said the 1995 ban on U.S. companies trading in Iranian oil had failed and Washington's attempt this year to punish foreign firms with ties to Tehran ran contrary to international law.

U.N. sanctions against Iraq, imposed after Saddam Hussein sent tanks into Kuwait, were also missing their target, having little impact if any on the regime or its leader and could return to haunt the West, Chalabi said.

"The continuation... of the sanctions can only harm further the Iraqi people and possibly cause more damage to existing oil facilities and the prospects of having more oil supplies from Iraq into the world market."
